subject: HISTORY
content_markdown:
FREEDOM STRUGGLE & MOVEMENTS

• Revolt of 1857
- **European Soldier to Indian soldier ratio**: 1:2
- Revolt of 1857 -> Proportion of Europeans to Indians was carefully fixed at 1:2 in the Bengal Army and 2:5 in the Madras and Bombay Armies to avoid another revolt (Peel Commission, 1859 / [NCERT](https://ncert.nic.in/)).
    - In Awadh, more {{hl}}than 20,000 taluqdars had their estates confiscated{{/hl}}

• Bengal Partition (1905)
- **Reason given for Partition**: Population of {{hl}}78 million{{/hl}} Bengal had become too big to be administered.

• Jallianwala Bagh
- House of Lords endorsed Reginald Dyer’s action and the British public showed solidarity with him by helping collect {{hl}}30,000 pounds{{/hl}} for him for his atrocities in Jallianwala Bagh.

• Non-Cooperation Movement (1920 to 1922)
- {{hl}}1st nationwide movement launched{{/hl}} by Gandhiji in 1920 during British rule.
- **During Non-cooperation Movement**:
    - Thousands of students left schools and colleges and joined only 800 national schools and colleges.
    - {{hl}}Rs 1 crore{{/hl}} were raised for Tilak Swaraj Fund by August 1921, and {{hl}}1 crore{{/hl}}/{{hl}}50 lakhs{{/hl}} members got enrolled in Congress.
- **Consequence of Non-Cooperation Movement**: The import of foreign goods halved between 1921 and 1922.

• Home Rule League Movement
- Tilak’s Home Rule League had 6 Branches while Annie Besant’s Home rule League had 200+ Branches.

• Civil Disobedience Movement (1930)
- Gandhi along with a band of 78 members of Sabarmati Ashram, marched from his headquarters in Ahmedabad for 240 miles.

• Administrative Reforms
- **Cornawallis Reforms**:
    - all higher posts in administration worth {{hl}}more than 500 pounds a year{{/hl}} in salary could be held by Englishmen only.
    - Charter Act of 1793 had reserved all posts worth 500 pounds per annum for the covenant servants of the Company.
    - Salary of the Collector of a district was raised to Rs. 1500 a month and {{hl}}1 per cent{{/hl}} commission on the revenue collected from his district.
- **Viscount Lee Commission** recommendations (1924): Parity between Indians and Europeans: To be achieved {{hl}}50:50 parity{{/hl}} in {{hl}}15 years{{/hl}}.
- **Morley-Minto Reforms**: number of members in the Central Legislative Council was raised from 16 to 60.
- **Provinces**: 3 provinces in 1773 to 17 provinces in 1947.

• Social Development
- **Status of illiteracy**: ~{{hl}}94%{{/hl}} in 1911 (~{{hl}}6%{{/hl}} literacy) and ~{{hl}}92%{{/hl}} in 1921 (~{{hl}}8%{{/hl}} literacy; ~{{hl}}84%{{/hl}} illiteracy at Independence in 1947) ([Census of British India](https://censusindia.gov.in/census.website/) / [NCERT](https://ncert.nic.in/))
    - **Number of Universities**:
        - **1857:** 3 (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras)
        - **1947:** 19 universities, ~500 colleges
    - **Age of Consent Act(1891):** Raised age of consent for girls from 10 to {{hl}}12 years{{/hl}}.
    - **Child Marriage Restraint Act (1929):** Minimum marriage age: 14 (girls) and 18 (boys).
    - **Gandhi ji campaign for untouchability**: Gandhi’s campaign against untouchability which covered 12,500 miles and lasted for nine months.
    - **Poona Pact**: Number of seats reserved for the depressed classes in provincial legislatures would be increased from 71 in the Award to 147; and to {{hl}}18%{{/hl}} of the total in central legislature.
    - **Rabindranath Tagore** wrote around 2230 songs.

- **Bilateral Trade**: ${{hl}}57 billion in 2024{{/hl}}

    - India was the UK's {{hl}}11th largest trading partner{{/hl}} in 2024, accounting for {{hl}}2.4% of total{{/hl}} UK trade.
    - Exports and Imports: India's exports stood at ${{hl}}8.5 billion{{/hl}} and imports were ${{hl}}3.7 billion.{{/hl}}
    - FDI: India is second-largest investor in terms of the number of FDI projects for the UK for five consecutive years.
    - Economic asymmetry: India's larger economy (${{hl}}4 trillion{{/hl}}) contrasts with UK's higher per capita income ($50,000 vs. $3,000).
- **India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA / FTA, effective 15 July 2026 - [MoC&I](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2290437®=48&lang=1)):**
    - It aims to double trade between the world’s fifth and sixth-largest economies in goods and services, increasing it from ${{hl}}60 billion{{/hl}} currently to ${{hl}}120 billion by 2030{{/hl}}.
- Grants zero-duty access for {{hl}}99%{{/hl}} of Indian exports to the UK (India's merchandise exports to the UK reached {{hl}}$13.44 billion ($13,444.19 million) in FY 2025-26{{/hl}}; additionally, the {{hl}}India–EFTA TEPA entered into force in October 2025{{/hl}} offering {{hl}}99.6%{{/hl}} Indian export coverage) ([MoC&I](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2290437®=48&lang=1) / [PIB July 2026](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2290437®=48&lang=1)).
    - Tariffs on automobiles will drop significantly, from over {{hl}}100 percent{{/hl}} to {{hl}}10 percent{{/hl}} under a special quota system
    - Expected outcomes:
        - ↑ UK’s GDP by £{{hl}}3.3 billion by 2035{{/hl}} and double bilateral trade from {{hl}}US$60 billion in 2024{{/hl}} to {{hl}}US$100 billion by 2030{{/hl}}.
        - ↑ bilateral trade, with projected annual growth of around {{hl}}15 percent{{/hl}} until calendar year 2030 [Care Edge report].

JUDICIARY

• Judges to Population Ratio
- {{hl}}~15–21 judges per million population{{/hl}} (15 working judges per million in India Justice Report 2025; ~21 sanctioned judges per million in Department of Justice data)
    - 150 per million – USA
    - Law Commission (India) -> 50 per million

• Low Female Representation
- **Supreme Court:** Till date, only 11 female judges in Supreme Court
- **High Court:** {{hl}}11.5%{{/hl}} Judges are female
- **Subordinate courts:** {{hl}}30%{{/hl}} Judges are women
- **Female Advocates:** Out of {{hl}}1.7 million{{/hl}} registered, only {{hl}}15%{{/hl}} are women

• Huge Pendency
- **Supreme Court:** 82,445 pending cases (Jan 2025)
- **High Courts and Subordinate courts:** {{hl}}>5.1 crore pending cases{{/hl}} across District/Subordinate Courts (~4.5+ crore) and High Courts (~{{hl}}62.98 lakh{{/hl}} as of April 2025), plus ~82,000+ in Supreme Court ([NJDG](https://njdg.ecourts.gov.in/) / [India Justice Report 2025](https://indiajusticereport.org/files/IJR%204_Full%20Report_English_Low.pdf))
• Extent of Problem
- {{hl}}1,514 cases in High Courts and 1,390 in subordinate{{/hl}} and district courts have been pending {{hl}}for over 50 years.{{/hl}}
- In {{hl}}subordinate courts, more than 50 per cent of cases{{/hl}} have been pending for over three years.
- **Government the Largest Litigant:** involvement of the Indian government as the largest litigant, contributing to {{hl}}50%{{/hl}} of pending cases.
- **Justice Delayed:** At the current disposal rate if no new cases added
- Supreme Court - {{hl}}1.3 years{{/hl}} and High Courts and Subordinate Courts – {{hl}}3 years{{/hl}}.
    - HC - {{hl}}21%{{/hl}} cases pending for over {{hl}}10 years{{/hl}}
    - Subordinate Courts - {{hl}}23%{{/hl}} cases for over five years

• Infrastructure Deficiency
- **Lack of Courtrooms:** shortage of 4,200 courtrooms for judges across the country (Centre for Research and Planning of Supreme Court of India report)
- **District courts**: ~{{hl}}37.7%{{/hl}} of Judicial Officers (JOs) have reported lack of adequate space in courtrooms.
- **Low Spending:** {{hl}}0.09% of GDP{{/hl}} to maintain the judicial infrastructure.
- **No Power Backup:** {{hl}}59%{{/hl}} of courtrooms
- **Toilets:** {{hl}}26%{{/hl}} of court complexes do not have separate ladies toilets and {{hl}}16%{{/hl}} do not have gents’ toilets.
- **Drinking water facility:** Only {{hl}}54%{{/hl}} of court complexes have purified drinking water facilities.
- **Record room:** Only {{hl}}32%{{/hl}} of courtrooms have separate Record Rooms.
- **Library:** Only {{hl}}51%{{/hl}} of court complexes have a library.
- **Video-conference Facility**: Only {{hl}}27%{{/hl}} of courtrooms have computers placed on the Judge’s dais with video-conferencing facilities.
    - {{hl}}50%{{/hl}} of lawyers, particularly in district courts, do not have any laptop or computer facility

• Lok Adalat
- National Lok Adalat settles {{hl}}1.45 crore{{/hl}} cases, prevents {{hl}}1.22 crore{{/hl}} new cases (2024)

• Gram Nyayalayas
- {{hl}}Target: 2500{{/hl}}
- **Limited implementation:** only 476 notified by just 15 states
- {{hl}}Operational: 314{{/hl}}
- **No GN in North East**

• Fast Track Special Courts
- {{hl}}745+ Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs){{/hl}}, including 404+ exclusive e-POCSO Courts, operational across 30 States/UTs (disposing >{{hl}}3.06 lakh{{/hl}} cases) ([Department of Justice, Ministry of Law & Justice](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseDetail.aspx?PRID=2295880®=6&lang=1))
    - collectively disposed of over 3,06,604 cases to date.
    - 1800 FTCs recommended by {{hl}}14th{{/hl}} Fin Commission

• Transparency Issues - Judges Asset Disclosure
- Out of 769 High Court judges, only 95 ({{hl}}12.35%{{/hl}}) have publicly disclosed their assets.
- Kerala High Court leads with {{hl}}18%{{/hl}} of its judges disclosing assets (41 out of 44), followed closely by Himachal Pradesh at {{hl}}91.66% {{/hl}}(11 out of 12).
- Chhattisgarh HC (1/16) and Madras HC (5/65) report some of the lowest disclosures.
- As of April 2025, 30 of 33 SC judges have declared their assets, and a Full Court resolution ensures all 33 will publish their declarations soon.

content_markdown:
BIOTECHNOLOGY AND HEALTH SCIENCES

• Biotechnology
- India is emerging as world leader in biotechnology
- Over {{hl}}11,000+ biotech startups{{/hl}} (up from 6,500+) and 75+ bio-incubators supported by DBT/BIRAC
- Union Budget 2026-27 also launched **Biopharma SHAKTI** with a {{hl}}₹10,000 crore{{/hl}} outlay over {{hl}}5 years {{/hl}}([India BioEconomy Report 2026](https://ableindia.in/manage/images/resourceuploads/_IBER%202026_compressed.pdf) / [Union Budget 2026-27](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2221455)).
- India's {{hl}}BioEconomy reached USD 195.3 billion in 2025{{/hl}} (up {{hl}}18%{{/hl}} from {{hl}}USD 165.7 billion in 2024{{/hl}} and {{hl}}USD 10 billion in 2014{{/hl}}), contributing {{hl}}nearly 5% (4.25–5%) to national GDP{{/hl}} and targeting ${{hl}}300 billion by 2030{{/hl}} ([BIRAC India BioEconomy Report 2026](https://ableindia.in/manage/images/resourceuploads/_IBER%202026_compressed.pdf))

• Human Genome Sequencing
- India completed sequencing 10,000 healthy genomes from different regions, representing 99 distinct populations.

• Immunization (WHO Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC) 2023)
• Global:
- Childhood immunization coverage stalled in 2023-> {{hl}}2.7 million{{/hl}} children either unvaccinated or under-vaccinated.
- Over {{hl}}50%{{/hl}} of unvaccinated children live in the 31 conflict-affected countries.
- **India:** In 2023, {{hl}}1.6 million{{/hl}} children missed crucial Diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus (together called DPT) and measles vaccinations.
- India accounted for {{hl}}2 million{{/hl}} zero-dose children.
- So far {{hl}}5.46 crore{{/hl}} children and {{hl}}1.32 crore{{/hl}} pregnant women have been vaccinated under Mission Indradhanush

• Neglected Tropical Diseases- Global report on Neglected Tropical Diseases 2024 (WHO)
- **Global Burden:** Over {{hl}}1 billion{{/hl}} people affected by NTDs
- {{hl}}1.6 billion{{/hl}} need preventive or curative interventions ([WHO](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091535)).
- **India’s Share**: accounts for ~{{hl}}40%{{/hl}} of the global population requiring NTD interventions—the highest worldwide.
• 2030 Targets ([WHO](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091535)):
- {{hl}}90%{{/hl}} reduction in the number of people needing NTD interventions.
- {{hl}}75%{{/hl}} reduction in vector-borne NTD-related deaths.
- **Mortality Trend:** Deaths from vector-borne NTDs increased by {{hl}}22%{{/hl}} in 2022 compared to 2016.
- **WASH Access:** {{hl}}85.8%{{/hl}} in NTD-endemic countries have WASH access overall, but only {{hl}}63%{{/hl}} among those needing NTD interventions.
- **India’s Achievements:** Certified free of Guinea Worm (2000) and Yaws (2016) by WHO.
- **Economic Cost:** Eliminating NTDs by 2030 could save over ${{hl}}342 billion{{/hl}} in healthcare costs and productivity losses ([WHO](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091535)).

• Rare Diseases
- In India, a disease is considered rare if it affects fewer than 1 in 2,500 individuals.
- Over {{hl}}70 million{{/hl}} Indians living with rare diseases

- **Patent applications:** Surged to {{hl}}1,43,729 patent applications filed in FY 2025-26{{/hl}} (and {{hl}}1,10,375 in FY 2024-25{{/hl}}, up from 58,503 in FY 2020-21; placing India in the {{hl}}global Top 6 for patent filings{{/hl}}) ([MeitY](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2291148®=48&lang=2) / [CGPDTM](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2260532®=6&lang=1) / [PIB May 2026](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2260532®=6&lang=1)).

• Disposal of patent application
- **Disposal of patent application:** In India, it takes about {{hl}}58 months{{/hl}} on average to dispose of a patent application ( {{hl}}20 months{{/hl}} in China and {{hl}}23 months{{/hl}} in US).

• Global rank
- **Global rank (GII):** India ranks {{hl}}38th out of 139 economies in the Global Innovation Index (GII) 2025 and GII 2026{{/hl}} (up from {{hl}}39th{{/hl}} in GII 2024 and {{hl}}81st{{/hl}} in 2015; ranks {{hl}}1st among 36 lower-middle-income economies{{/hl}} and {{hl}}1st globally{{/hl}} in ICT services exports) ([WIPO GII 2026](https://www.wipo.int/gii-ranking/en/india))

HUNGER, POVERTY & INEQUALITY

• Poverty

• India - Poverty
- **Percentage**: {{hl}}21.9%{{/hl}} {2011, Tendulkar Report}
- **Extreme poverty:** Under the World Bank's revised International Poverty Line ($3.00/day at 2021 PPP, up from $2.15/day), India's extreme poverty rate stood at {{hl}}5.3% in 2022-23{{/hl}} (and {{hl}}23.9%{{/hl}} at the lower-middle-income line) [[World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/country/india) / [Economic Survey 2025-26](https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/doc/echapter.pdf)]
• Decrease in Poverty [[World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/country/india)]
- **Extreme Poverty Lift:** 171 Million lifted from Extreme Poverty in last decade.
- **India’s Poverty Rate** (at the 3.65 dollars per day line)-> Fell from {{hl}}61.8 percent in 2011{{/hl}}-12 to {{hl}}28.1 percent in 2022{{/hl}}-23.
    - **Rural poverty** declined from {{hl}}69 percent{{/hl}} to {{hl}}32.5 percent{{/hl}}
    - **Urban poverty** dropped from {{hl}}43.5 percent{{/hl}} to {{hl}}17.2 percent{{/hl}}.
- **Non-monetary poverty (Multidimensional Poverty Index - MPI)** -> declined from {{hl}}55.3%{{/hl}} in 2005-06 to {{hl}}11.28% in 2022-23{{/hl}} ({{hl}}24.82 crore{{/hl}} people escaped multidimensional poverty in {{hl}}9 years{{/hl}}) ([NITI Aayog](https://www.niti.gov.in/sites/default/files/2023-08/India-National-Multidimentional-Poverty-Index-2023.pdf) / [Economic Survey 2025-26](https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/doc/echapter.pdf)) [[UNDP](https://hdr.undp.org/) MPI: {{hl}}53.8%{{/hl}} in 2005-06 to {{hl}}16.4%{{/hl}} in 2019-21].

• Global - Poverty
- **Incidence**: {{hl}}8.5% of total{{/hl}} population i.e. {{hl}}75 cr{{/hl}} live in extreme poverty - on less than $2.15 per day [[World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/country/india)]
- **Deprived Regions:** 5 out of 6 poor are in Sub-Saharan or South Asia
- **Rural > Urban** – over {{hl}}75%{{/hl}} of all poor live in rural areas.
- **High Prevalence among Children (< 18):** {{hl}}50% of total{{/hl}} poor

• Inequality
• Oxfam Report - Global
- The richest {{hl}}1%{{/hl}} control {{hl}}45% of global{{/hl}} wealth.
• Oxfam Report - India
- Richest {{hl}}1%{{/hl}} control more than {{hl}}40% of total{{/hl}} wealth
- Bottom {{hl}}50%{{/hl}} own merely {{hl}}3%{{/hl}}
• Gini Coefficient
- The Gini coefficient improved for rural areas (declined to 0.237 in 2023-24 from 0.266 in 2022-23) and urban areas (declined to 0.284 in 2023-24 from 0.314 in 2022- 23).
- **Rural-Urban Divide:** Average Monthly Per Capita Expenditure (MPCE) -> Rs. 4, 122 (Rural) and Rs. 6,996 (Urban) ([Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2023-24](https://www.mospi.gov.in/publications-reports)).

• Hunger
• Status of Hunger [[Global Hunger Index 2024](https://www.globalhungerindex.org/pdf/en/2025.pdf)]
• Global
- {{hl}}2.8 billion{{/hl}} people cannot afford a healthy diet.
• India Specific
- **India's Rank:** Improved to {{hl}}102nd out of 123 countries in Global Hunger Index 2025{{/hl}} (up from {{hl}}105th{{/hl}} out of 127 in GHI 2024; remains in the "serious" category) [[GHI 2025](https://www.globalhungerindex.org/pdf/en/2025.pdf)]
    - **Child Wasting Rate**: {{hl}}18.7% {{/hl}}[Highest in World]
- **Stunted Children**: {{hl}}32.9% in GHI 2025{{/hl}} ({{hl}}29.3%{{/hl}} in UN SDR 2026; down from >{{hl}}35%{{/hl}} earlier; Child Wasting at {{hl}}18.7%{{/hl}}) [[GHI 2025](https://www.globalhungerindex.org/pdf/en/2025.pdf)]
    - {{hl}}Under-5 mortality{{/hl}}: {{hl}}2.9%{{/hl}}
- Status of Food Security [[State of Food Security and Nutrition Report (2024)](https://www.fao.org/publications/home/fao-flagship-publications/the-state-of-food-security-and-nutrition-in-the-world)]
• India Specific
- **Undernourished**: {{hl}}13%{{/hl}} from Chronic Undernourishment
- **Anemic**: {{hl}}53%{{/hl}} of Women
• UN-FAO Report
- Hunger in India came down to {{hl}}13.7%{{/hl}} during 2021-23 period

content_markdown:
HEALTH

• Mental Health
• India
- **Lifetime prevalence** of mental disorders in India is {{hl}}13.7%{{/hl}}.
- {{hl}}10.6% of adults{{/hl}} in India suffer from mental disorders (National Mental Health Survey (NMHS) 2015-16)
• Mental Health in Students
- {{hl}}23% of school{{/hl}} children have mental health problems (NIMHANS study)
- {{hl}}27.8%{{/hl}} of undergraduate students had mentalhealth conditions and {{hl}}31.3 per cent{{/hl}} of postgraduate students had suicidal thoughts.
- **Self-reporting rate**: <{{hl}}1% {{/hl}}(IIT Jodhpur study)
- **Treatment gap:** {{hl}}70-92%{{/hl}}
- **Economic Loss:** B/w 2012-2030, is estimated at {{hl}}USD 1.03 trillion {{/hl}}([WHO](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091535))
• Mental health professionals
- Only 0.75 psychiatrists, 0.07 psychologists and 0.07 social workers per {{hl}}1 lakh{{/hl}} people.
- India short of 27,000 psychiatrists to reach the recommended ratio of 3 per {{hl}}1 lakh{{/hl}} people.
- **Mental healthcare budget & initiatives**: Govt spends ~{{hl}}0.05% of GDP{{/hl}} (~{{hl}}1.1%{{/hl}} of health budget) on mental health; {{hl}}Union Budget 2026-27 announced setting up NIMHANS-2 in North India{{/hl}} and upgrading National Mental Health Institutes in Ranchi and Tezpur as Regional Apex Institutions ([Union Budget 2026-27](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2221455)).
• Global
- {{hl}}13.9% of population{{/hl}} experience mental disorders
- India (0.75 psychiatrists per lakh people) vs Developed countries (6.6 psychiatrists per 100,000 people).

• Traditional Medicines
• India
- **Medicinal plants market**-> {{hl}}Rs. 4.2 billion in 2019{{/hl}}; expected to increase at CAGR of {{hl}}38.5%{{/hl}} to {{hl}}Rs. 14 billion by 2030{{/hl}}.
- 8,000 herbal remedies codified in AYUSH systems; {{hl}}Union Budget 2026-27 announced 3 new All India Institutes of Ayurveda{{/hl}} (Ministry of AYUSH / [Union Budget 2026-27](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2221455)).
    - **Ayush exports:** ${{hl}}18 billion{{/hl}}
• Global
- {{hl}}80%{{/hl}} of the population use traditional medicine.
- Global herbal medicine market is projected to grow from ${{hl}}153.5 billion in 2022{{/hl}} to ${{hl}}279.8 billion in 2028{{/hl}}.

• Tobacco Consumption
• India
- {{hl}}2nd largest consumer{{/hl}} and producer of tobacco
- **Usage:** {{hl}}42% of men{{/hl}} and {{hl}}14% of women{{/hl}} in India use tobacco (GATS2 data)
- **Deaths:** In India, nearly 3600 people die every day due to tobacco use.
• Economic loss
- India loses {{hl}}1%{{/hl}} of its GDP to diseases and early deaths from tobacco use ([WHO](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091535))
- For every Rs 100 received as excise taxes from tobacco products, the economy loses Rs 816.
- **Wastage:** {{hl}}1.7 lakh tonnes{{/hl}} of waste every year.
• Global
- 1 in every 10 cigarettes and tobacco products consumed globally is illicit.
- {{hl}}22.3%{{/hl}} of the world's population used tobacco ([WHO](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091535))

• Rural Health
- There is shortage of {{hl}}83.2%{{/hl}} of surgeons, {{hl}}74.2%{{/hl}} of obstetricians and gynaecologists, {{hl}}79.1%{{/hl}} of physicians, {{hl}}81.6%{{/hl}} of paediatricians in rural areas.
- Only {{hl}}45.1%{{/hl}} PHCs function on a 24×7 basis.
- Of the 5,480 functioning CHCs, only 541 have all four specialists.

EDUCATION

• Brain Drain
- B/w 2015 and 2022, {{hl}}1.3 million{{/hl}} Indians left.
- **Citizenship renounced:** 225,000 Indians renounced their citizenship (2022).
- **Economic loss:** India’s IT industry could have added ${{hl}}15-20 billion{{/hl}} more annually had the talent stayed.
- {{hl}}75%{{/hl}} of emigrating Indians choose to stay back after studies completion.

• Exam Leaks
- 70 exam leaks in the last {{hl}}7 years{{/hl}} across 15 states.

WOMEN

• Social Issues

• CRIMES (Marital Rape)
- {{hl}}2%{{/hl}} of married women face physical, sexual or emotional violence by their husbands.
- India is one of only 36 countries where marital rape is not criminalized.

VULNERABLE SECTIONS

• Child Marriage
- {{hl}}23.3% of women{{/hl}} aged {{hl}}20–24 years{{/hl}} were married before age 18 in NFHS-5 (2019-21); as per {{hl}}SRS Statistical Report 2024{{/hl}}, the mean age at effective marriage for females rose to {{hl}}23.1 years{{/hl}}, with only {{hl}}2.1% of females marrying before age 18{{/hl}} in 2024 ([ORGI SRS 2024](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/47152/download/51396/SRS_STAT_2024.pdf)).
    - {{hl}}17.7% of men{{/hl}} aged {{hl}}25-29 years{{/hl}} were married before age {{hl}}21 years{{/hl}}.
    - Prevalence reduced by half from {{hl}}47% {{/hl}}(2006) to {{hl}}23.3% {{/hl}}(2019-21).
    - Total cases registered under Child Marriage Act -> 1050 (2021) ([NCRB](https://ncrb.gov.in/)).
    - Every minute, three girls are forced into child marriage ['India Child Protection' research team study].

• Child Artist
- B/w 6,059 and 12,334 child artists [Study by Child Rights and You].
- Child artists in films and TV work for over 12 hours a day.

• Schools
- **Government Schools:** {{hl}}38.11% {{/hl}}({{hl}}27.8 lakh{{/hl}})
- **Unaided Schools:** {{hl}}60.75% {{/hl}}({{hl}}44.31 lakh{{/hl}})
- **School Enrolment**:↓ {{hl}}37 lakh in 2023{{/hl}}-24 compared to previous year [[UDISE data](https://udiseplus.gov.in/)].

• Higher Education Level
- **Gross Enrollment Ratio (GER) ->** 0.4 in 1950-51 to 28.4 in 2021-22.
- **Student Enrolment:** Over {{hl}}4 crore{{/hl}} students, making India the second- largest after China.
- **Target for GER**: National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 aims for {{hl}}50%{{/hl}} by 2035
- World {{hl}}2nd Largest{{/hl}} Higher Education system
- **Girls with Higher Education**: Enrolment of women in Indian universities grew {{hl}}26%{{/hl}} in 2024.
- **Vulnerable Sections**: Enrollment among OBCs increased by {{hl}}80.9%{{/hl}}, SC enrollment grew by {{hl}}76.3%{{/hl}}.
- **Stream wise Ratio**:
    - Humanities ({{hl}}33%{{/hl}}), Science ({{hl}}15%{{/hl}}), Commerce ({{hl}}14%{{/hl}}), English ({{hl}}12%{{/hl}})
- **Pupil-Teacher Ratio (PTR)**: Steady at 23:1 for the last five years.
- **University Density (per 1 lakh eligible students):** Highest in Sikkim (10.3), Arunachal Pradesh (5.6), Ladakh (5.2), etc. In Bihar (0.2), UP (0.3), West Bengal & Maharashtra (0.6) the density is below national average.

• Expenditure
• Government Spending:
- **Expenditure**: {{hl}}2.9% of GDP{{/hl}}
- {{hl}}Target under NEP 2020{{/hl}}: {{hl}}6% of GDP{{/hl}}
- **Budgetary allocation (2026-27):** {{hl}}₹1.39 lakh crore (₹1,39,289.48 crore){{/hl}} allocated to the Ministry of Education in Union Budget 2026-27 (including {{hl}}₹83,562 crore{{/hl}} for School Education and {{hl}}₹55,727 crore{{/hl}} for Higher Education), an {{hl}}8.27% hike{{/hl}} over {{hl}}₹1.28 lakh crore in 2025{{/hl}}-26 ([Union Budget 2026-27](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2221455)).

• Infrastructure
• Inefficient Infrastructure [[UDISE+ 2023-24 Report](https://udiseplus.gov.in/)]
- **Computers:** The percentage of schools having computers ↑ from {{hl}}38.5 %{{/hl}} in 2019-20 to {{hl}}57.2 %{{/hl}} in 2023-2024.
- **Internet:** Percentage of schools having internet facility increased from {{hl}}22.3 %{{/hl}} in 2019-20 to {{hl}}53.9 %{{/hl}} in 2023-2024.
- **Electricity:** Of the over {{hl}}14.71 lakh{{/hl}} schools in India, up to {{hl}}1.52 lakh{{/hl}} schools have no functional electricity.
- **Drinking Water**: While {{hl}}14.47 lakh{{/hl}} schools claim to have drinking water facilities, only {{hl}}14.11 lakh{{/hl}} have them functional.

HEALTH

• Health GDP%
• Government Spending:
- ~{{hl}}1.84–1.9% of GDP{{/hl}} (Union Budget 2026-27 increased allocation for Ministry of Health & Family Welfare by {{hl}}10%{{/hl}} to {{hl}}₹1,06,530.42 crore{{/hl}} for FY 2026-27) ([Economic Survey](https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/doc/echapter.pdf) / [Union Budget 2026-27](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2221455))
- World Average = {{hl}}6%{{/hl}}
- Target = {{hl}}2.5% {{/hl}}[National Health Policy, 2017]
• Economic Survey (2024-25)
- **Share of government health spending in total health expenditure** increased to {{hl}}48 per cent in 2022{{/hl}} from {{hl}}29 per cent in 2015{{/hl}}.
- In FY 2022, India spent {{hl}}₹9.04 lakh crore{{/hl}} on health—{{hl}}3.8% of GDP{{/hl}}-> ₹6,602 per person.

• Health of Poverty
• Out of Pocket Expenditure (OoPE):
- **Decrease in OoPE:** OOPE as a percentage of total health expenditure (THE) declined from {{hl}}62.6%{{/hl}} in 2014-15 to {{hl}}39.4%{{/hl}} in 2021-22 [[National Health Accounts (NHA) Estimates](https://nhsrcindia.org/national-health-accounts-records)]
- **People Pushed into Poverty:** {{hl}}6 crore{{/hl}} people pushed into poverty every year, due to OoPE [[NITI Aayog](https://www.niti.gov.in/sites/default/files/2023-08/India-National-Multidimentional-Poverty-Index-2023.pdf)]

• Human Resource
• Availability of Doctors and Nurse:
- **Public Sector**: Only {{hl}}10%{{/hl}} of doctors are in the Public Sector.
- **Doctor/Population:** 1: 834 v/s 1: 1000 ([WHO](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091535) recommended)
    - {{hl}}112%{{/hl}} increase in MBBS seats (since 2014)
    - Allopathic doctors to population — 1 doctor/1,194 people.
- **Nurse/Population Ratio:** 1.96 per 1,000 [[WHO](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091535) recommended 3 per 1,000]

• Infra/Inputs
- **Bed: Patient:** 1.3/1000 v/s 3: 1000
    - Delhi: 2.7/1000
- **Increase in Colleges:** {{hl}}82%{{/hl}} increase in Medical Colleges (since 2014)
• Institutional deliveries [[MoHFW](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseDetail.aspx?PRID=2246870®=1&lang=1)]
- ↑ from {{hl}}79% {{/hl}}(NFHS-4, 2015-16) to {{hl}}88.6% (~89%) in NFHS-5 (2019-21){{/hl}}, and further to {{hl}}95.4% of deliveries receiving medical attention in 2024{{/hl}} [[MoHFW](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseDetail.aspx?PRID=2246870®=1&lang=1) / [ORGI SRS Statistical Report 2024](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/47152/download/51396/SRS_STAT_2024.pdf)].
- {{hl}}100%{{/hl}} in Kerala, Goa, Lakshadweep, Puducherry and Tamil Nadu and more than {{hl}}90%{{/hl}} in eighteen other States/UTs.
• Import Dependency:
- **Active Pharma Ingredients** (API)
    - {{hl}}70-80%{{/hl}} imported from China
    - Indian API market projected to reach ${{hl}}21.2 billion by 2033{{/hl}}.
- **Medical Equipments**: ~ {{hl}}75%{{/hl}} are imported

• Insurance

• Insurance Penetration
- **Low Insurance Penetration**: {{hl}}3.7%{{/hl}} in FY24 [Global average: {{hl}}7%{{/hl}}]
    - **Life Insurance penetration**: dropped marginally from {{hl}}3 %{{/hl}} in FY23 to {{hl}}2.8 %{{/hl}} in FY24 [[Economic Survey 2024–25](https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/)]
    - **Non-life insurance** remained at {{hl}}1%{{/hl}}.
- India ranks {{hl}}10th{{/hl}} in the global life insurance market.

• Insurance Coverage
- **Health Insurance**: {{hl}}37%{{/hl}} covered under Health Insurance Schemes.
- **Without Health Insurance**: {{hl}}90 crore{{/hl}} Indians lack access to health Insurance [[IRDAI data](https://irdai.gov.in/annual-reports)]

• Health Insurance Sector
- **Market size:** {{hl}}6th largest insurance market{{/hl}} by 2032 ([Swiss Re report](https://www.swissre.com/institute/research/sigma-research/sigma-2026-01-natcat-2025-wildfire-storm-risk.html))
- **Density:** $91 insurance density (global avg $874)
- **Insurance Premium:** Total insurance premium grew from {{hl}}₹8.3 lakh crore in FY21{{/hl}} and {{hl}}₹11.2 lakh crore in FY24{{/hl}} to {{hl}}₹11.9 lakh crore in FY25{{/hl}} ([Economic Survey 2025-26](https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/doc/echapter.pdf))

• Rural Areas Variations
- **Rural Areas**: ≈ {{hl}}20%{{/hl}} of Total Hospital
- **Shortage of Manpower in Rural Areas [[Union Ministry of Health data](https://mohfw.gov.in/)]**
    - **Doctors:** {{hl}}70%{{/hl}} shortage of specialist doctors
    - **Primary Health Centres:** Shortfall of {{hl}}3.1%{{/hl}} of allopathic doctors ([Rural Health Statistics 2021-2022](https://mohfw.gov.in/))
    - **Rural Community Health Centres:** maximum for surgeons ({{hl}}73 per cent{{/hl}}) followed by physicians ({{hl}}69 per cent{{/hl}}), paediatricians ({{hl}}68 per cent{{/hl}}) and Obs & Gyn specialists ({{hl}}61 per cent{{/hl}})

• Disease Burden
- **Non communicable disease:** 2/{{hl}}3rd{{/hl}} of total deaths
    - {{hl}}5.8 million{{/hl}} Indians die from NCDs each year
    - 1 in 4 Indians faces the risk of dying from NCD before reaching age of 70.
- **TB:** {{hl}}26.07 lakh{{/hl}} TB cases in 2024, marking highest notified cases ever.
- {{hl}}India among 10 countries{{/hl}} that make up {{hl}}60 % of global{{/hl}} maternal deaths, still births, new born deaths (UN)
- {{hl}}Mortality Rate [Sample Registration System (SRS) Statistical Report 2024 (released May 2026) & 2021-23 Bulletin]{{/hl}}
- **MMR:** {{hl}}88–93 per lakh live births{{/hl}} (reduced by {{hl}}86%{{/hl}} since 1990, outpacing the global {{hl}}48%{{/hl}} reduction; 93 in SRS 2019-21) ([ORGI SRS](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/47152/download/51396/SRS_STAT_2024.pdf) / [Economic Survey 2025-26](https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/doc/echapter.pdf))
- **NMR:** {{hl}}18–19 per 1,000 live births{{/hl}} ({{hl}}70%{{/hl}} decline during 1990–2023 vs {{hl}}54%{{/hl}} globally) ([ORGI SRS](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/47152/download/51396/SRS_STAT_2024.pdf) / [Economic Survey 2025-26](https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/doc/echapter.pdf))
- **IMR:** Declined to {{hl}}24 per 1,000 live births in 2024{{/hl}} (down from 25 in 2023, 27 in 2021, and 40 in 2013; lowest in Kerala at 8) ([ORGI SRS Statistical Report 2024](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/47152/download/51396/SRS_STAT_2024.pdf))
- **U5MR:** Declined to {{hl}}28 per 1,000 live births in 2024{{/hl}} (down from 29 in 2023 and 31 in 2021; {{hl}}78%{{/hl}} reduction since 1990 vs {{hl}}61%{{/hl}} globally) ([ORGI SRS Statistical Report 2024](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/47152/download/51396/SRS_STAT_2024.pdf))
• Anaemia ([NFHS 5](https://mohfw.gov.in/)):
- 2/3 or {{hl}}67% of children{{/hl}}
- 1/2 or {{hl}}57% of women{{/hl}}
- 1/4 or {{hl}}25%{{/hl}} of Men
- 3 in 4 Indian women have low dietary iron intake.

• Obesity
- **India**: {{hl}}3rd most obese country{{/hl}}
    - **Urban** – {{hl}}70%{{/hl}} of Obese people
- {{hl}}1/4 Indian{{/hl}} is Obese ([NFHS 5](https://mohfw.gov.in/))
    - {{hl}}22.9% of men{{/hl}} and {{hl}}24% of women{{/hl}} are obese.
    - % of overweight children under five increased to {{hl}}3.4%{{/hl}} from {{hl}}2.1%{{/hl}} in NFHS-4 (2015-16) at the all-India level.
- **Definition:** WHO defines it as abnormal fat accumulation with:
    - BMI > 30 -> Obese
    - BMI 25-30 -> Overweight
- **Economic cost:** {{hl}}USD 28.95 billion {{/hl}}(Rs 1,800 per capita)
    - By 2030 ↑ to Rs 4,700 per capita or {{hl}}1.57% of GDP{{/hl}}.
• Global
- One-third of children worldwide will be obese by 2050 [Lancet Study]
- {{hl}}211 crore{{/hl}} obese individuals in 2021 ({{hl}}45%{{/hl}} of the world’s population).

• Open Defecation
- **Lack of Toilet Access:** {{hl}}20%{{/hl}} do not have access to toilet {1 in 5 household practice open deficiency} – NFHS 5
- **World Bank** – {{hl}}11 %{{/hl}} of India’s Population practice open defecation.

WOMEN

• Economic Empowerment

• Wage Gap
- Indian women earn Rs 40 for every Rs 100 men earn ([WEF](https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_GGGR_Report_2026.pdf))
- **India rank**: {{hl}}131st out of 145 countries in Global Gender Gap Index 2026{{/hl}} (parity score {{hl}}64.5%{{/hl}}; was {{hl}}131st{{/hl}} out of 148 countries with {{hl}}64.1–64.4%{{/hl}} score in GGGI 2025) ([WEF Global Gender Gap Report 2026](https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_GGGR_Report_2026.pdf))

• Labor Force Participation
- **India**: The female LFPR has risen from {{hl}}23.3 %{{/hl}}(2017- 18) to {{hl}}41.7%{{/hl}}(2023-24). ([Eco survey 2024-25](https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/)).
- **Global:** Women's global labour force participation rate stood at {{hl}}48.7 per cent in 2023{{/hl}} ([ILO](https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@dgreports/@dcomm/@publ/documents/publication/wcms_711919.pdf)).

• Women in Informal Sector
- More than {{hl}}95%{{/hl}} women working in Informal sector ([ILO](https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@dgreports/@dcomm/@publ/documents/publication/wcms_711919.pdf))

• Finance Availability to Women
- {{hl}}80% of women{{/hl}} run enterprises are self-financed
- < {{hl}}5%{{/hl}} borrowed money from some financial institutions.

• Global Gender Gap Report 2025 & 2026 (WEF)
- **India's Gender Parity Score**: {{hl}}64.5% in 2026{{/hl}} (vs global average of {{hl}}69.2%{{/hl}}; India scored {{hl}}96.6%{{/hl}} in Educational Attainment, {{hl}}95.6%{{/hl}} in Health & Survival, {{hl}}41.2%{{/hl}} in Economic Participation, and {{hl}}24.5%{{/hl}} in Political Empowerment) [{{hl}}64.1–64.4%{{/hl}} in 2025] ([WEF GGGR 2026](https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_GGGR_Report_2026.pdf))
- **India rank:** {{hl}}131/145 in GGGR 2026{{/hl}} (131/148 in GGGR 2025) ([WEF GGGR 2026](https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_GGGR_Report_2026.pdf))
- **South Asia**: Bhutan (119), Nepal (125), and Sri Lanka (130) ranked better than India.
- **Gender Parity Timeline:** At the current pace, it will take {{hl}}~120 years{{/hl}} globally to achieve full gender parity in GGGR 2026 (down from {{hl}}134 years{{/hl}} earlier) ([WEF GGGR 2026](https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_GGGR_Report_2026.pdf)).

• Social Issues

• Education
- **Literary Rate**: {{hl}}65.46% {{/hl}}([2011 Census](https://censusindia.gov.in/census.website/))
- **Worldwide:** {{hl}}12.2 crore{{/hl}} girls remain out of school globally [[UNICEF](https://www.unicef.org/india/)]
- **Gender Parity in Secondary Education**: India showed the best gender parity in terms of enrolment in secondary education [[Global Gender Gap report, 2024](https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_GGGR_2025.pdf)]

• Health (NFHS-5)
- **TFR:** {{hl}}2.0 in NFHS-5 (2019-21){{/hl}} and declined further to {{hl}}1.9 in SRS Statistical Report 2024{{/hl}} (below replacement level of 2.1) ([NFHS-5](https://mohfw.gov.in/) / [ORGI SRS 2024](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/47152/download/51396/SRS_STAT_2024.pdf))
- **Anaemia**: {{hl}}57% of women aged 15–49 years{{/hl}} are anaemic in India ([NFHS-5](https://mohfw.gov.in/)) [~1 in 3 globally]

• CRIMES
- India records {{hl}}51 cases{{/hl}} of crime against women every hour ([NCRB](https://ncrb.gov.in/))
- 1/{{hl}}3rd crimes{{/hl}} by husband/relative ([MoSPI](https://www.mospi.gov.in/uploads/latestReleases/latest_release_1767781372753_1380ce82-f5a5-440d-99e6-e6b35af0deb5_GDP_Press_Note_on_FAE_2025-26.pdf))
- **Cybercrime**: reporting surged by {{hl}}25%{{/hl}}
- **Suicides**: {{hl}}4.2%{{/hl}} Increase ([NCRB, 2022](https://ncrb.gov.in/crime-in-india.html))
• Rape
- {{hl}}4th most common crime{{/hl}} against women

• Population
- **World population:** ~{{hl}}57% of global{{/hl}} population lives in urban areas (UN World Urbanization Prospects / [World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/country/india))
- **Population (India Urban Share)**: {{hl}}31.16% {{/hl}}({{hl}}37.7 crore{{/hl}}) in Census 2011 -> ~{{hl}}36.4% {{/hl}}(~52+ crore) in 2024–2025 -> projected to reach ~{{hl}}40% {{/hl}}(~{{hl}}60 crore{{/hl}}) by 2036 ([Census 2011](https://censusindia.gov.in/census.website/) / [World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/country/india) / [MoHUA](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2298526))
    - Increase of {{hl}}40%{{/hl}} by 2036 – World Bank
- **GDP contribution** = {{hl}}63%{{/hl}}
    - Increase to {{hl}}70%{{/hl}} by 2036 – World Bank
- **Growth Rate:** India urban population for 2022 was 50.8 Cr, a {{hl}}2.05%{{/hl}} increase from 2021 ([World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/country/india)).

• Slums
- **Census 2011 - Total Population in Slums:** {{hl}}6.55 cr{{/hl}} Indians live in Slums (around {{hl}}5%{{/hl}})
    - Maharashtra ({{hl}}1.18 cr{{/hl}}) > Andhra Pradesh ({{hl}}1.02 cr{{/hl}})
- **Cities with >10 Lakh Population:** over {{hl}}29%{{/hl}} population living in slums (EPW).
    - Bombay (over {{hl}}34%{{/hl}}, Calcutta {{hl}}32%{{/hl}}, Madras {{hl}}32%{{/hl}} and Delhi {{hl}}31%{{/hl}}).
    - {{hl}}65%{{/hl}} of Indian cities have adjoining slums.

• Homeless
- {{hl}}Census 2011{{/hl}} - {{hl}}0.15% of population{{/hl}} (17-18 lac)
- **Commissioners of SC -** {{hl}}1%{{/hl}} of the urban population is homeless (~{{hl}}37 lakhs{{/hl}}).
- **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs:** approx {{hl}}23.93 lakh{{/hl}} people are homeless.

• Migration
- **Total Migration Rate** = {{hl}}28.9% {{/hl}}([Migration in India report, 2020-21](https://www.mospi.gov.in/publications-reports))
    - **Rural Areas** - {{hl}}26.5 %{{/hl}}
    - **Urban Areas -** {{hl}}34.9%{{/hl}}
    - {{hl}}Employment: 10.8%{{/hl}} persons were migrated for employment related reasons
    - **Females:** {{hl}}47.9% {{/hl}}- ({{hl}}48%{{/hl}} in rural and {{hl}}47.8%{{/hl}} in urban areas)
        - **Main reason – Marriage:** {{hl}}86.8%{{/hl}} females migrated for marriage
    - **Males:** {{hl}}10.7% {{/hl}}- ({{hl}}5.9%{{/hl}} in rural and {{hl}}22.5%{{/hl}} in urban areas)
        - **Main reason – Employment:** {{hl}}49.6%{{/hl}} of males migrated for employment
- **Domestic migrants:** ↓ {{hl}}12%{{/hl}} to {{hl}}40.20 crore{{/hl}} between 2011 and 2023 [[EAC-PM](https://eacpm.gov.in/)].

• Miscellaneous
- **Open Defecation:** Over {{hl}}25%{{/hl}} rural households defecate in the open in contrast to Swachh Bharat data ([NFHS-5](https://mohfw.gov.in/))

- **World Bank** – {{hl}}100%{{/hl}} of Urban Population has access to electricity.
